title: Talking to children during an emergency
def: Children take their cue from adults; calm, simple, honest words and a job to do help them feel safer.
look: a child clinging, crying, or very quiet
questions repeated many times
trouble sleeping after the event
use: Get down to their level, say what is happening in a few words, tell them what you are doing to keep them safe, and give them a small task.
not: Do not share frightening details or let them watch hours of disaster coverage.

title: Reuniting a family after a storm or evacuation
def: After a disaster, families reunite fastest when everyone knows the meeting places and the out-of-area contact ahead of time.
look: the planned meeting spot
an out-of-area contact who relays messages
official reunification or shelter registries
use: Go to the planned meeting place, text the out-of-area contact, and register with official shelters or reunification services.
not: Do not return to a damaged or evacuated area to search until officials say it is safe.

title: School or daycare pickup when phones or roads fail
def: A pickup plan names who can collect each child, how the school will reach you, and what happens if roads or phones are down.
look: the school's emergency and release policy
backup adults on the authorized pickup list
the school's alert sign-up
use: Learn the school's plan, add backup adults to the pickup list, and tell children who may collect them.
not: Do not rush to a school in lockdown; follow official instructions about where to reunite.

title: Child carriers and trail safety with little ones
def: Hiking with a baby or toddler needs a carrier that fits both of you, extra warmth and sun protection for the child, and short, flexible plans.
look: the child's face, hands, and feet staying warm or shaded
the carrier's weight limit
secure footing on descents
use: Check the child often, dress them warmer than you since they are not moving, take breaks, and avoid steep or icy ground.
not: Do not hike exposed ridges or icy trails with a child on your back.

title: Shared kit: who carries the meds and the inhaler
def: In a group, life-saving medicines such as an epinephrine auto-injector or an inhaler must stay with the person who needs them, with a backup someone else knows about.
look: an epinephrine auto-injector with the allergic person
a spare inhaler with another adult
a list of medicines and doses
use: Decide before leaving who carries what, show others where it is, and keep medicines protected from heat and freezing.
not: Do not pack someone's emergency medicine in a car or another person's bag that may not be nearby.
call: Use epinephrine as prescribed for a severe allergic reaction and call 911.

title: Pets in a power outage, heat, or cold
def: Pets suffer in heat and cold like people do; during an outage they need shade or warmth, water, and their food and medicines.
look: heavy panting, drooling, or weakness in heat
shivering or lethargy in cold
spoiled pet food after an outage
use: Keep pets indoors with you, give plenty of water, never leave them in a parked car, and bring them when you go to a warming or cooling center that accepts pets.
not: Do not leave pets tied outside in a storm or extreme weather.
call: Call your veterinarian for heatstroke or cold injury signs.

title: Helping children after a hard event
def: After a close call, a death, or seeing an animal harvested, children need brief, age-appropriate words, honest answers, and permission to have feelings.
look: questions, drawings, or play about the event
clinginess or nightmares
a return to normal play over days
use: Answer simply and honestly, keep routines, and let them talk or not; tell them it is okay to feel sad or confused.
not: Do not lecture or force a child to talk.
call: Ask a pediatrician or counselor if distress lasts more than a few weeks.

title: Youth seasons and mentored hunts
def: Many states have youth days or apprentice licenses with special rules on age, supervision, and hunter education; they change by year.
look: the state's minimum age and supervision distance
a hunter-education course requirement
special youth season dates
use: Read your state agency's current youth-hunting page and follow its supervision rules.
not: Do not rely on rules from a past year or another state.

title: Supporting a teenager in crisis
def: A teenager in crisis needs an adult who listens calmly, takes their words seriously, and connects them with help.
look: withdrawal, giving things away, or talk of death
sudden changes in sleep, school, or friends
access to guns or medicines
use: Listen without judging, ask directly about suicide if worried, lock up guns and medicines, and call or text 988 together.
not: Do not promise secrecy about safety or wait for it to pass.
call: Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Emergency contact and medical card
def: A small paper card with emergency contacts, allergies, medicines, and conditions helps responders when a phone is locked or dead.
look: names and numbers of two contacts
allergies, medicines, and conditions
a copy in wallet, kit, and car
use: Make a card for each family member, update it when medicines change, and add emergency contacts to your phone's lock-screen medical info.
not: Do not rely on a locked phone alone.

title: Checking on older relatives and neighbors
def: Older adults are at higher risk in heat, cold, and outages, especially if they live alone or rely on medical devices.
look: no answer by phone during an outage or heat wave
confusion, weakness, or a cold or hot home
medicines or devices that need power
use: Call or visit twice a day during extreme weather or outages, help them reach a cooling or warming center, and make sure they have water and medicines.
not: Do not assume they are fine because they say so on the phone if the home is very hot or cold.
call: Call 911 for confusion, collapse, or trouble breathing.

title: Children and water
def: Drowning is quick and silent; children need a watcher whose eyes stay on them and a life jacket near open water.
look: a designated adult watcher with no phone
a properly fitted life jacket
cold or moving water
use: Name one adult watcher at a time, keep young children within arm's reach, and use life jackets on boats and near rivers and ponds.
not: Do not rely on floaties or assume a child will splash or shout if in trouble.
call: Call 911 for any child pulled from water, even if they seem fine.
